findings.claim: A TikTok/social media spat with Marks & Spencer drove huge free publicity.
findings.truth: The 2021 Cuthbert the Caterpillar row began when Marks & Spencer lodged an intellectual property claim against Aldi in the High Court in April 2021; Aldi's playful reply won the free publicity, and the case was settled in February 2022. It was not a TikTok spat.

findings.claim: When BrewDog set a 2030 carbon-negative target, it agreed to invest heavily in land restoration and renewable energy.
findings.truth: BrewDog had no 2030 carbon-negative target. It claimed carbon-negative status from 2020 and wound that claim down in 2024, so it is no longer a safe example. The verified investment is at the Ellon brewery: treatment plants, biogas technology and, since 2021, an anaerobic digestion plant.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, BrewDog (Ellon brewery; 'Why BrewDog is winding down its carbon negative claim', July 2024)

findings.claim: In 2020 the UK fashion retailer Boohoo faced accusations that its Leicester suppliers paid staff far below the minimum wage - sales fell, share price dropped sharply, and the company commissioned an independent review.
findings.truth: Boohoo's sales did not fall. Revenue rose through 2020 (first-quarter revenue up 45%) and kept growing the following year. What fell was the share price, by about 46%. The independent review by Alison Levitt QC reported in September 2020.
The minimum single-use carrier bag charge in England has been 10p since 21 May 2021, and it applies to retailers of every size, not just large ones.
findings.evidence: gov.uk, Carrier bag charges: retailers' responsibilities

findings.claim: Charging 5p for carrier bags (also: plastic-film takeback, reusable cup discounts).
findings.truth: Same as F4: the England minimum charge is 10p.
findings.evidence: gov.uk, Carrier bag charges: retailers' responsibilities

findings.claim: The exam will always ask you to weigh both sides.
findings.truth: An invented exam claim. Both papers open with multiple-choice and short-answer questions worth 20 marks in total, where 1-mark and 2-mark items ask for recall, not balance. Only the higher-tariff questions ask students to weigh both sides.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 assessment (Paper 1 and Paper 2, Section A worth 20 marks)

findings.claim: In 2022-2024 the Bank of England lifted interest rates from 0.1% to 5.25% to fight inflation.
findings.truth: Bank Rate was 0.1% from 19 March 2020. The rises began on 15 December 2021 and reached 5.25% on 2 August 2023. 2024 brought cuts, not rises: the rate was 5% by 21 August 2024. The correct window is 2021 to 2023.

findings.claim: Between 2022 and 2024, how far did the Bank of England raise its base rate?
findings.truth: Same as F7: the rise ran from December 2021 to August 2023. The answer (0.1% to 5.25%) is right; the dates in the question are wrong.

findings.claim: One mark for any two of the following: (heading of the 2-mark 'Give two ways' mark scheme in L3 Q2, and again in L5 Q2)
findings.truth: The heading reads as one mark for two points. The bullets each carry [1 mark] and the total is [2 marks], so the intent is clear; 'one mark for each of any two' would be exact. Wording only, no fact or tariff is wrong.
findings.evidence: recomputation against the stated [2 marks] total

findings.claim: a UK firm reaching 300 million customers in Europe has far more room to grow than one selling only to 67 million Britons
findings.truth: The EU population is about 452 million (1 January 2026), and wider Europe is larger still. 300 million understates the market a UK exporter can reach.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Demographics of the European Union (451,990,314 at 1 Jan 2026)

findings.claim: 'A strong pound is usually good news for which of the following?' - the marked answer is 'A UK manufacturer importing German steel', but option 2 is 'A UK holiday firm taking customers to Spain who pay in pounds'.
findings.truth: A holiday firm that takes payment in pounds and buys Spanish hotel rooms in euros also gains from a strong pound, so the question has two correct answers and marks a right choice wrong. The lesson itself makes this point in reverse: when the pound fell after 2016, holiday firms' costs rose. Replacing the option with a UK hotel chain relying on US visitors makes it unambiguously bad news under a strong pound.
findings.evidence: SPICED applied to the firm's own trade direction; L4 content_html paragraph n16

findings.claim: examiners want you to explain the effect on a business, not recite dates and section numbers
findings.truth: The substance is right but the attribution to examiners is invented. The specification is the source: 'Only brief knowledge of each law is needed. More emphasis should be placed on the effects of the legislation on businesses.'

findings.claim: Businesses that pay less face fines and public naming by HMRC - as Argos, Superdrug and even Marks & Spencer have all discovered in recent years.
findings.truth: Two small points. HMRC investigates and fines; the naming lists are published by the government department for business. Argos and Marks & Spencer have both appeared on naming rounds; Superdrug could not be confirmed on any round within this session's fetch allowance, so it is left alone rather than corrected.
findings.evidence: not verified - WebSearch budget exhausted, gov.uk naming rounds not fetched

summary: Five lessons, 13 findings, 11 edits. Exam framing is sound throughout: every practice tariff is a real AQA tariff (1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 12), no paper or section is misnamed, no SPaG claim, and both 'not required' spec rules (no exchange-rate calculations, no interest-rate theory) are stated correctly. The 37.5% percentage-change key and the £100 at $1.25/$1.40 exchange worked example both recompute, and SPICED runs the right way round everywhere. One knowledge check in L4 had two correct answers; the rest are date and figure errors (Bank Rate window, 5p bag charge, Boohoo sales, BrewDog target, EU market size) plus two invented exam-voice claims. Note for the applier: the L2 and L5 descriptions are already over the 100-character validator limit (109 and 110) and were not written by this pass.
